From the late 1700s to the late 1900s, resistance to foreign rule changed a lot in its goals but less in its methods. Early resistance in places like India in 1857 was often about restoring older rulers and traditions, while later movements in the 1900s wanted independent nation-states based on ideas of self-determination. However, armed struggle stayed common the whole time, even as new methods like mass nonviolent campaigns and political parties appeared.

To understand this, it helps to look at the bigger picture. In the late 1700s, Enlightenment thinkers like John Locke and Rousseau argued that government should be based on the consent of the people, and these ideas helped spark the Atlantic Revolutions. Then in the 1800s, industrialization gave European countries the steamships, railroads and weapons they needed to expand empires, and at the Berlin Conference of 1884-1885 European powers divided Africa among themselves. Later, the two world wars weakened Britain and France, and colonial soldiers who fought for them came home expecting more rights. All of this shaped what resistance movements wanted and how they fought.

One early example is the Haitian Revolution, which began in 1791. Enslaved Africans in Saint-Domingue rose up against the French, and under leaders like Toussaint Louverture they fought for the end of slavery and eventually independence, which came in 1804. Haiti shows that Enlightenment ideas about liberty could be used against the empire that spread them, so in some ways it looks forward to later nationalism. But its method was armed revolt, which was the main way people resisted at this time.

The Indian Rebellion of 1857 shows a different goal. Indian soldiers called sepoys rebelled against the British East India Company, partly because of rumors that new rifle cartridges were greased with cow and pig fat, which offended Hindus and Muslims. Many rebels rallied around the old Mughal emperor in Delhi, so their goal was more about restoring an older order than creating a new nation. The British crushed the rebellion and then took direct control of India in 1858. Similarly, the Maji Maji Rebellion in German East Africa used spiritual beliefs that special water would protect fighters from bullets. These movements were local and looked backward.

By the 1900s goals had clearly changed. The Indian National Congress, founded in 1885, started out asking for more Indian participation in government, but under Gandhi it became a mass movement demanding full independence. Gandhi used nonviolent methods such as the Salt March in 1930 and boycotts of British cloth, which brought millions of ordinary people into the struggle. India gained independence in 1947. This was a big change from 1857 because the goal was a modern Indian nation and the method was mass civil disobedience instead of a military uprising.

Still, armed struggle continued. In Algeria, the FLN fought a brutal war against France from 1954 to 1962 because France saw Algeria as part of France and had a large settler population that refused to leave. Nonviolence was harder to use where settlers were so powerful. So the goal was the same as India's, an independent nation, but the method was closer to Haiti's. Ghana, on the other hand, gained independence in 1957 mostly through political organizing and strikes led by Kwame Nkrumah, showing that methods depended on how the colonial power responded.

Overall, the goals of resistance shifted from restoring older orders or ending specific abuses toward building independent nation-states, which was a major change caused by spreading nationalist ideas and the weakening of empires after the world wars. Methods changed less, because while mass politics and nonviolence were new, armed revolt remained common wherever colonizers refused to leave.

Resistance to foreign rule changed a lot between 1750 and today in both its goals and its methods, but some things stayed the same because people always wanted to be free from outsiders. Early on, resistance was mostly about getting rid of foreign rulers by fighting, while later it became more about building nations and using mass politics, although fighting never completely went away.

In the 1700s and 1800s, many people resisted foreign rule because they were angry about how they were treated. The Haitian Revolution is a good example. Enslaved people in Haiti rose up against French rule and fought a long war until Haiti became independent in 1804. This shows that armed revolt was a main method in this time, and the goal was freedom from France.

Later on, resistance changed in some ways. People started to use more peaceful methods and organized larger groups of people. Resistance became more organized and had more support from ordinary people. The goals also changed because people wanted their own countries and governments. Still, some movements kept using violence, so there is continuity in the methods.

In conclusion, the goals and methods of resistance to foreign rule changed over time but also stayed similar in some ways. People wanted freedom and used different ways to get it, and this was true in many places around the world.
